4.11 Capital Market Assumptions

Why history is not enough

Section titled “Why history is not enough”

Asset allocation and long-term planning need assumptions about the future expected returns, volatilities and correlations of asset classes; this set of numbers is called capital market assumptions. The simplest approach is to use historical average returns, but 4.10 Estimation Error and Robust Optimization showed that their errors are large: even with decades of data, the standard error of the average return is several percentage points.

Historical averages have another problem: they include changes in valuation. If P/E ratios rose from 10 to 25 over a period, part of that period’s stock return came from investors being willing to pay more for the same earnings. That part cannot be expected to repeat: it requires P/E ratios to keep rising at the same pace.

Check C1
US stocks earned a high average return over the past 40 years, part of which came from a large rise in P/E ratios. Using this 40-year average directly as the expected future return amounts to assuming that P/E ratios will keep rising at the same pace.
Think: what pieces can the historical return be split into? If P/E ratios stop rising, which piece disappears?

So in practice forward-looking methods are common: estimate future returns from today’s prices, yields and economic growth, and use historical data for volatilities and correlations (which are estimated far more precisely).

Building blocks

Section titled “Building blocks”

The building-block approach splits the expected stock return into pieces (Grinold and Kroner, 2002):

E[R]≈y+g+π+ΔvE[R] \approx y + g + \pi + \Delta vE[R]≈y+g+π+Δv
  • yyy, the shareholder yield: the dividend yield plus the net buyback yield (buybacks minus newly issued shares).
  • ggg, the real growth of earnings per share: bounded in the long run by real economic growth (2.2 Long-Run Growth), and new companies and new share issues make per-share growth lower than the growth of the whole economy.
  • π\piπ, inflation: earnings and dividends broadly rise with prices. Leaving out this piece gives the real expected return (Fisher equation).
  • Δv\Delta vΔv, the valuation change: if the P/E ratio is expected to go from PE0PE_0PE0​ to PEnPE_nPEn​ over nnn years, the yearly contribution is about (PEnPE0)1/n−1\left(\frac{PE_n}{PE_0}\right)^{1/n} - 1(PE0​PEn​​)1/n−1.

Bonds are much simpler: over a holding period close to the duration, a bond portfolio’s return is about its starting yield to maturity (3.4 Interest Rate Risk), so the starting yield is a good estimate of the expected return; for corporate bonds, expected default losses must also be subtracted (3.6 Credit Risk).

Check C2
In Figure 2-1, set the P/E in 10 years equal to today's (30), then raise inflation from 2.5% to 4.5%, keeping everything else the same. By the building-block approach:
The real return is the nominal return minus inflation. If inflation and the nominal return both rise 2 points, what happens to the real return?
The building-block approach assumes earnings and dividends rise with prices. Does the inflation piece enter the nominal return?
Look at the readout: the inflation piece is added to the nominal return.

Valuation and future returns

Section titled “Valuation and future returns”

The hardest block to estimate is the valuation change. The cyclically adjusted P/E (CAPE) of 3.11 Equity Valuation III: Relative Valuation gives some clues: historically, when CAPE was high, average returns over the next 10 years tended to be low, and when it was low they tended to be high (Campbell and Shiller, 1998). In US data, CAPE clearly helps explain returns over the next 10 years but explains almost nothing about returns over the next year.

This relation needs care:

  • There are few observations. Monthly 10-year returns overlap, and since 1881 there have been only a dozen or so non-overlapping 10-year periods (Exercises Question 4).
  • The “normal” CAPE may have changed: accounting rules, buybacks replacing dividends and the industry mix (more technology companies) can all change CAPE’s long-run level. Since the 1990s, US CAPE has mostly been above its long-run average.
  • How long it takes valuations to return to average cannot be known.
Check C3
CAPE has clear explanatory power for returns over the next 10 years and almost none for the next year. The most reasonable implication is:
CAPE explains almost none of the next year's return. What would adjusting holdings every year by it achieve?
The 10-year returns of neighboring months overlap almost completely. How many truly independent 10-year periods are there?
Think of the joint hypothesis problem (4.7 The Efficient Market Hypothesis): must predictable long-run returns be mispricing? What else could they be?

The equilibrium approach

Section titled “The equilibrium approach”

Another approach does not forecast but asks: what expected returns do today’s market prices imply? If the market portfolio is optimal in the mean–variance sense (4.3 The Capital Allocation Line and the Capital Market Line), one can work back to the expected returns that make it optimal; this is called reverse optimization (Sharpe, 1974):

Π=δ Σ wmkt\Pi = \delta\,\Sigma\,w_{\text{mkt}}Π=δΣwmkt​

wmktw_{\text{mkt}}wmkt​ is the vector of market-value weights, Σ\SigmaΣ the covariance matrix, δ\deltaδ the market’s risk aversion (which can be estimated as the market risk premium divided by the market variance), and Π\PiΠ the implied expected excess returns. Asset iii‘s implied return equals δ\deltaδ times its covariance with the market portfolio, consistent with the CAPM (4.4 The Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM)).

Check C4
The implied expected returns from reverse optimization are forecasts of future returns and must be more accurate than historical averages.
Think: under what assumptions are implied returns derived? If the market portfolio is not optimal, or the CAPM does not hold, are they still accurate forecasts?

The implied returns are themselves a reasonable, mutually consistent set of expectations: optimizing with them gives the market portfolio, without the extreme weights of 4.10 Estimation Error and Robust Optimization. The Black–Litterman model (Black and Litterman, 1992) builds on this by adding the investor’s own views: the result is a weighted average of equilibrium returns and views, with weights set by confidence in the views. With a single asset,

μBL=Π/τσ2+Q/ω1/τσ2+1/ω\mu_{\text{BL}} = \frac{\Pi / \tau\sigma^2 + Q / \omega}{1 / \tau\sigma^2 + 1 / \omega}μBL​=1/τσ2+1/ωΠ/τσ2+Q/ω​

QQQ is the view, ω\omegaω the uncertainty (variance) of the view, and τσ2\tau\sigma^2τσ2 the uncertainty of the equilibrium return. This is the same idea as the shrinkage estimator of 4.10 Estimation Error and Robust Optimization: equilibrium returns are the reference value toward which estimates are shrunk.

Check C5
Why are the results of the Black–Litterman model usually more stable than plugging the investor's own expected-return estimates straight into the optimizer?
Does the equilibrium return Π=δΣwmkt\Pi = \delta\Sigma w_{\text{mkt}}Π=δΣwmkt​ contain the covariance matrix?
It gives the market portfolio only when there are no views. What happens when views are added?
The model only sets how much weight views get; it does not judge whether they are right. Where does the stability come from?

Comparing with institutions

Section titled “Comparing with institutions”

Many asset managers publish their long-term capital market assumptions every year, for example J.P. Morgan’s Long-Term Capital Market Assumptions and Vanguard’s economic and market outlook. Most combine building blocks, valuation and the equilibrium approach to give expected returns and volatilities for asset classes over the next 10 to 15 years.

When using these forecasts, note that different institutions’ expectations for the same asset class can differ by several percentage points; they are point estimates with large uncertainty behind them (Vanguard and others give a range); and they change every year with market valuations. A sensible approach is to treat them as references, compare them with one’s own building-block estimates and find out which block the differences come from; to plan with a range rather than a single number; and to check how sensitive the conclusions are to the assumptions.

Summary

Section titled “Summary”
  • Historical averages have large errors and include valuation changes that cannot repeat; expected returns need forward-looking methods, while volatilities and correlations can come from historical data.
  • Building blocks: E[R]≈y+g+π+ΔvE[R] \approx y + g + \pi + \Delta vE[R]≈y+g+π+Δv (shareholder yield, real earnings growth, inflation, valuation change); a bond’s expected return is about its starting yield.
  • CAPE has some power to explain 10-year returns and almost none for 1 year; observations are few, and the “normal” level may change.
  • Reverse optimization Π=δΣwmkt\Pi = \delta\Sigma w_{\text{mkt}}Π=δΣwmkt​ gives implied returns consistent with the market; Black–Litterman averages views with equilibrium returns according to confidence.
  • Institutional forecasts differ considerably; planning should use ranges and sensitivity analysis.

Exercises

Section titled “Exercises”
Question 1
A financial adviser doing retirement planning for a client says: "US stocks have returned about 10% a year on average over the past 100 years, so we'll use 10%." Suppose today: dividend yield 1.4%, net buyback yield 0.6%, real growth of earnings per share 1.8%, expected inflation 2.5%, and CAPE at 30.
(a) If CAPE returns to 22 over the next 10 years, how much does the valuation change contribute each year? By the building-block approach, what is the nominal expected annual return? What if CAPE stays at 30?
(b) Evaluate the adviser's approach. How should these estimates be used in planning?
Question 2
A bond fund has a modified duration of about 6 and a yield to maturity of 3.2%. Rates suddenly rise 1 percentage point, and the fund's yield to maturity becomes 4.2%. An investor says: "Bonds just lost a lot of money, so bond returns look bad for the next few years; I'm selling."
(a) About how much does the fund's price change when rates rise? If rates stay put afterwards, about what is the fund's expected return each year from then on? After roughly how many years does the fund's cumulative return catch up with the path it would have followed if rates had not changed?
(b) Evaluate the investor's statement.
Question 3
The market has only two asset classes, stocks and bonds, with market weights of 60% and 40%. Stocks have a volatility of 16% and bonds 6%, with a correlation of 0.2, and the risk aversion is δ=3\delta = 3δ=3.
(a) Use Π=δΣwmkt\Pi = \delta\Sigma w_{\text{mkt}}Π=δΣwmkt​ to find the two asset classes' implied expected excess returns (use decimals for the variances and covariance).
(b) Another analyst plugs historical average excess returns (7% for stocks, 3% for bonds) straight into mean–variance optimization (with the same covariances and δ\deltaδ) and gets 73% in stocks and 239% in bonds (requiring borrowing). Why is the result so extreme? How does Black–Litterman handle the analyst's view that bonds will earn a fairly high return?
Question 4
A research report says: "Using monthly data from 1881 to 2024, we regress the annualized return over the next 10 years on CAPE: about 1,600 observations, with an R² of 0.4. With so many observations, the conclusion is very reliable. By this relation, investors should cut stocks when CAPE is above 25 and add stocks when it is below 15."
(a) About how many non-overlapping 10-year periods are there in this span? Why do overlapping observations make the conclusion look more reliable than it is?
(b) Since the late 1990s, US CAPE has often been above 25. Evaluate the rule "cut stocks when CAPE is above 25", and explain how CAPE is better used.
